[A1] The force field is prescribed and smooth on an open set of future timelike velocities, is orthogonal to the velocity argument, and $m,c>0$.

[F1] Picard–Lindelöf: “a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time” ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

[F2] Smooth dependence: for a jointly smooth field, near base data “there are a compact time interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$” on which the solutions exist and depend smoothly on initial data and parameters ([[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]).

[F3] Along a curve, $\frac{d}{ds}g(V,W)=g(D_sV,W)+g(V,D_sW)$ ([[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]]).

[F4] Every IVP satisfying Picard–Lindelöf has a “unique maximal solution” on an “open interval containing the initial time” ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]).

[F5] A nonzero causal vector is future-directed exactly when its pairing with the time-orientation field is negative, and that pairing cannot vanish ([[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]).

[F6] The covariant derivative along a curve is the pullback connection ([[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]); chart connection coefficients are defined by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).


## Proof

1.1 In a chart write $U=U^c\partial_c$. The pullback connection and its Leibniz rule in [F6] give $D_sU=(\dot U^a+\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\dot x^bU^c)\partial_a$; since $\dot x^b=U^b$, the covariant system is $\dot x^a=U^a$, $\dot U^a=-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(x)U^bU^c+m^{-1}f^a(x,U)$. The right side is smooth on an open chart-state domain, hence locally Lipschitz; [F1] gives a unique local solution through each allowed initial datum, and uniqueness makes coordinate solutions agree on chart overlaps. [given, F1, F6, algebra]

1.2 Along this solution, metric compatibility [F3] gives $\frac{d}{ds}g(U,U)=2g(D_sU,U)=2m^{-1}g(f(x,U),U)=0$ by [A1]. Thus $g(U,U)$ stays equal to its initial value $-c^2$. The vector $U$ never vanishes; by [F5] its continuous pairing with the time-orientation field cannot vanish, so the initially negative pairing remains negative and its future direction is preserved. [given, A1, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 The coordinate field is jointly smooth in initial coordinates and any smooth force parameters, so [F2] supplies smooth dependence on a common compact local interval. The maximal-solution theorem [F4] unions the unique local solutions into one maximal solution on an open interval; it asserts no infinite lifetime. [step 1.1, F2, F4] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^8$ be an open coordinate-state domain with state $z=(x,U)\in\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4$, and let $G:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^8$ be the smooth autonomous coordinate vector field of the shell-tangent force system in [[lem-rpm-shell-tangent-force-ivp]]. Let $z:(a,b)\to\mathcal D$ be its unique maximal solution. If $b<\infty$ and there are $b_0\in(a,b)$ and a compact set $K\subset\mathcal D$ such that $z([b_0,b))\subseteq K$, then the solution extends beyond $b$, contradicting maximality. The analogous statement holds at a finite left endpoint. Therefore a finite maximal endpoint can occur only if the state eventually leaves every compact subset of its open coordinate-state domain.

This is a mathematical continuation criterion for the coordinate ODE. It asserts neither that a solution exists for all proper times nor that the background spacetime is geodesically complete.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth coordinate-state domain and vector field in the Statement, the unique maximal shell-force solution, and the compact-tail hypothesis at a finite endpoint.

[L1] For a smooth force field orthogonal to the future timelike velocity on an open chart-state domain, each normalized future-timelike initial datum has a unique local solution; its norm and future direction are preserved, and the solution has a unique maximal open interval ([[lem-rpm-shell-tangent-force-ivp]]). The current in-run carrier is a draft and this lemma uses exactly that inspected interface conditionally.

[L2] For a differentiable vector curve with integrable derivative, its increment is the integral of its derivative ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]).

[L3] The norm of a vector-valued integral is at most the integral of its norm on a forward interval ([[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]]).

[L4] The coordinate solution is $C^1$ and satisfies $z'=G\circ z$; hence $G\circ z$ is a continuous vector function, its components are continuous and integrable on each compact parameter interval, and the vector-valued integral is defined componentwise ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** use bounded speed on the compact tail to obtain an endpoint state and apply local existence there.

1.1 Since $G$ is continuous and $K$ is compact, $M:=\max_{w\in K}\|G(w)\|_2$ is finite. By [L4], $G\circ z$ is vector-integrable on every compact subinterval. For $b_0\le s<t<b$, [L2] and [L3] give $\|z(t)-z(s)\|_2=\|\int_s^t G(z(r))\,dr\|_2\le\int_s^t\|G(z(r))\|_2\,dr\le M(t-s)$. Thus $z(t)$ is Cauchy as $t\uparrow b$ and has a limit $z_b\in\mathbb R^8$; because $K$ is compact and closed and the tail lies in $K$, $z_b\in K\subset\mathcal D$. [given, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 By [L1], the same smooth shell-force system has a local solution $\widetilde z$ through $z(b)=z_b$ at parameter $b$. The old solution extends continuously to $b$ by step 1.1. Taking the limit in its integral equation shows that the extension satisfies $\dot z=G(z)$ up to $b$ with left derivative $G(z_b)$; $\widetilde z$ has the same value and derivative at $b$. Gluing the old curve on $[b_0,b]$ to $\widetilde z$ just after $b$ therefore gives a solution extending beyond $b$, and local uniqueness in [L1] makes this extension agree with the original on overlaps. This contradicts maximality. Applying the same argument to the reversed parameter proves the left-endpoint case. [step 1.1, L1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The conclusion is local to the chosen chart-state domain. A finite endpoint can still arise by leaving that open domain or every compact subset of it; no global-lifetime claim follows.

## Statement

For $q\in(0,1)$, the bosonic geometric law on $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with weights $(1-q)q^n$ has mean $q/(1-q)$ and variance $q/(1-q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1+\mathbb E[n])$; its relative standard deviation tends to $1$ as $q\uparrow1$. The fermionic two-state law on $n\in\{0,1\}$ with weights $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$ has mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1-\mathbb E[n])$. Here Bose and Fermi name these explicitly specified counting laws; no claim about a physical preparation is made.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** The geometric and two-state laws with $q\in(0,1)$.

[A1] The bosonic states are $\mathbb N_0$ with weights proportional to $q^n$; the fermionic states are $\{0,1\}$ with weights proportional to $q^n$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]: countable canonical weights normalize when the partition sum is finite, and under the envelope the mean and variance follow from derivatives of $Z$.

[F2] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], [[def-expectation-on-a-finite-probability-space]], and [[def-variance-and-covariance]]: finite laws normalize and define means and variances by finite sums.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: every $q\in(0,1)$ has the form $e^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma=-\log q>0$.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule]]: derivatives of the parameterized exponential and logarithm compositions obey the chain rule.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: $n^k e^{-bn}\to0$ for each fixed integer $k$ and $b>0$.



## Proof

**Given:** The geometric and two-state laws with $q\in(0,1)$.

1.1 Let $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nq^n$. Multiplying this finite sum by $1-q$ gives $(1-q)S_N=1-q^{N+1}$. Since $q=e^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma>0$, [F5] gives $q^{N+1}\to0$; hence $Z=(1-q)^{-1}$ and the weights $(1-q)q^n$ sum to one. On a compact $\gamma$-interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, set $a_n=(1+n^2)e^{-bn}$. Then $a_{n+1}/a_n=e^{-b}(1+(n+1)^2)/(1+n^2)\to e^{-b}<1$. Choose $c$ with $e^{-b}<c<1$; for all sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le ca_n$, so the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series. Thus $\sum_n(1+n^2)e^{-\gamma n}\le\sum_na_n<\infty$, which is the local envelope required by [F1]. [A1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 The fermionic partition sum is $1+q$; its two probabilities are $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$. Their finite weighted sums give mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2$, equal to the mean times one minus the mean. [A1, F2, F3]

2.1 With $Z(\gamma)=(1-e^{-\gamma})^{-1}$, [F1] gives $\mathbb E n=-\partial_\gamma\log Z=q/(1-q)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(n)=\partial_\gamma^2\log Z=q/(1-q)^2$. Substitution $q=e^{-\gamma}$ and [F4] justify the parameter derivatives. Therefore $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(n)}/\mathbb E n=1/\sqrt q\to1$ as $q\uparrow1$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 These are calculations for the two specified probability laws only; no independence, physical preparation, or measured fluctuation claim is used. [A1, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $\beta,z>0$, let $\rho>0$ be an interior attainable density, and choose $\alpha=\log z$ supporting the free canonical rate $F_\beta$ at $\rho$. For either free or periodic boundary condition $b$, let $C^b_{L,N_L}$ be the exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ the grand-canonical law using the same finite-volume energy, where $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. Assume
$$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$
Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]], and let
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
Then for every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ there is $c_U>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log C^b_{L,N_L}\{\,\omega:R_{L,\omega}\notin U\,\}\leq-c_U.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$ under $C^b_{L,N_L}$. This is a statement about spatially averaged local observables through the empirical field, not about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A superstable regular interaction, $\beta,z>0$, an interior density $\rho$, exact particle numbers $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, the displayed canonical rate limit, and the same finite-volume boundary condition in the canonical and grand-canonical laws.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: the canonical and Poisson-normalized partition conventions satisfy $Z_{Q,b}(L,N;\beta)=e^{-L^d}Z_b(L,N;\beta)$ for either boundary condition.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-grand-duality]]: a supporting $\alpha=\log z$ gives physical pressure $P(\alpha,\beta)=F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho$.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]]: the normalized grand pressure is $p_Q(z,\beta)=P(\alpha,\beta)-1=-\min_P\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}$, and its minimizer set is nonempty and compact in $\tau_L$.

[F4] [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] and [[lem-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field-stationary-density]]: $R_{L,\omega}$ is the stationary empirical field used by the grand empirical-field large-deviation principle.

[L1] Georgii's Theorem 2 (1994, Sections 3–5) gives, for superstable regular interactions, a good large-deviation principle in $\tau_L$ for these periodized empirical fields under both free and periodic grand-canonical Gibbs laws, with rate $I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z+p_Q(z,\beta)$. The complete proof was read; the chosen $b$ must be one of the two stated boundary conditions.

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 The canonical law is the grand law conditioned on $N=N_L$, since the grand weight on the $N_L$ sector differs from the canonical density only by the constant activity factor $z^{N_L}$. Its conditioning probability is $$G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)=\frac{z^{N_L}e^{-L^d}Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)}{Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)}.$$ Divide the logarithm by $L^d$. The numerator terms tend to $\rho\log z+F_\beta(\rho)-1$ by the assumed canonical rate and [F1]; the denominator tends to $p_Q(z,\beta)$. By [F2]–[F3], $p_Q(z,\beta)=F_\beta(\rho)+\rho\log z-1$, so $$L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the exact-number conditioning event has subexponential, positive grand probability for all sufficiently large $L$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Let $U$ be an open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ and set $F=U^c$. The good rate in [L1] has zero set exactly $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. Its infimum on the closed set $F$ is strictly positive: otherwise a sequence in $F$ with rates tending to zero would lie in a compact rate sublevel, have a limit in $F$, and by lower semicontinuity that limit would be a zero of the rate outside $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. The large-deviation upper bound therefore gives some $c>0$ with $$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}\leq-c.$$ [F3, F4, L1, algebra]

2.1 Conditioning on $N=N_L$ yields $$C^b_{L,N_L}\{R_{L,\omega}\notin U\}\leq \frac{G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}}{G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)}.$$ The numerator decays exponentially by step 1.2 and the denominator has zero exponential rate by step 1.1, so the ratio tends to zero. This proves concentration on every neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. If the minimizer is unique, these neighborhood bounds are exactly convergence in probability in $\tau_L$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. For $x,y\in U$, suppose the whole segment $[x,y]$ lies in $U$ and its concavity inequality holds:

$$f(x+t(y-x))\ge(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad(0\le t\le1).$$

Then the supporting bound is $f(y)\le f(x)+Df(x)(y-x)$. In particular this bound holds for every $x,y$ in any convex subset of $U$ on which $f$ is concave. No global convexity of $U$ is assumed.

Let $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ be linear, $b\in\mathbb R^k$, and $F=U\cap\{x:Ax=b\}$. Suppose $x_*\in F$, $Df(x_*)h=0$ for every $h\in\ker A$, and for every $y\in F$ the segment $[x_*,y]$ lies in $U$ and has the displayed concavity inequality. Then $x_*$ is a global maximum of $f$ on $F$. If $F$ is convex and $f|_F$ is strictly concave, meaning the inequality is strict for distinct endpoints and $0<t<1$, the maximum is unique.

For the curvature clause, suppose $f\in C^2(U)$ and fix $x\in U$. If, for every $h\in\mathbb R^d$, all sufficiently small $|t|$ satisfy $x\pm th\in U$ and

$$f(x+th)+f(x-th)\le2f(x),$$

then the Hessian bilinear form $D^2f(x)=D(Df)(x)$ satisfies $D^2f(x)[h,h]\le0$ for every $h$. This condition holds whenever $f$ is concave on a neighborhood of $x$. Thus a $C^2$ function concave on an open convex region has negative-semidefinite Hessian there. Concavity alone does not assert strict curvature.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open domain, differentiability, and the stated admissible segments and concavity inequalities; affine constraints and stationarity for the maximum clause; strict concavity or $C^2$ regularity only for their respective further clauses.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: every segment between points of a convex set stays in that set.

[F2] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]: $f(x+h)=f(x)+Df(x)h+o(\|h\|)$ at each point of differentiability.

[F3] [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: continuous first and second coordinate partials give total derivatives of $f$ and its vector of first partials; thus a $C^2$ function restricted to the line $t\mapsto x+th$ is $C^2$, with second derivative $D^2f(x+th)[h,h]$.

[F4] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a real function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable inside it has an interior derivative equal to its endpoint secant slope.

## Proof

1.1 For an admissible pair $x,y$ and $0<t<1$, the given concavity inequality yields $f(y)-f(x)\le(f(x+t(y-x))-f(x))/t$. By [F2] the right side tends to $Df(x)(y-x)$ as $t\downarrow0$, proving the supporting bound. The convex-region specialization follows from [F1] and the concavity inequality on that region; it does not require any other segment of $U$ to be admissible. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For $y\in F$, linearity gives $A(y-x_*)=0$, so stationarity yields $Df(x_*)(y-x_*)=0$. The assumed segment from $x_*$ to $y$ permits step 1.1, hence $f(y)\le f(x_*)$, proving global maximality. If $F$ is convex and two distinct points maximize $f$, their midpoint lies in $F$ by [F1], while strict concavity would give a strictly larger midpoint value. Thus the maximum is unique under the further hypothesis. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Under the $C^2$ and local midpoint hypotheses, fix $h$ and put $g(t)=f(x+th)$ near zero. By [F3], $g''(0)=D^2f(x)[h,h]$. Define $R(t)=g(t)-g(0)-g'(0)t-\tfrac12g''(0)t^2$. Differentiability of $g'$ gives $R'(s)=o(|s|)$; [F4] on the interval between $0$ and $t$ gives $R(t)=tR'(\xi_t)=o(t^2)$, since $|\xi_t|\le|t|$. Therefore $(g(t)+g(-t)-2g(0))/t^2\to g''(0)$. Its numerator is nonpositive by hypothesis, so $D^2f(x)[h,h]\le0$. Concavity on a neighborhood implies that midpoint hypothesis on every sufficiently short centered segment; this proves all Hessian claims without strengthening the domain assumptions. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ be linear, let $b\in\mathbb R^k$, and let $x_*\in U$ satisfy $Ax_*=b$. Put $T=\ker A$. Assume $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable and has second directional derivatives represented by a continuous matrix field: there is a continuous map $H:U\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with symmetric values, and for every $x\in U$ and $h\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}f(x+th)\right|_{t=0}=Q_x(h):=h^{\mathsf T}H(x)h.$$

Assume stationarity $Df(x_*)h=0$ for every $h\in T$. If $Q_{x_*}(h_0)<0$ for some $h_0\in T$, then $x_*$ is not a local minimum of $f$ on $\{x\in U:Ax=b\}$. If $Q_{x_*}(h)>0$ for every nonzero $h\in T$, then $x_*$ is a strict local minimum on that feasible slice. If $T=\{0\}$, the latter conclusion holds because $x_*$ is the only feasible point.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open convex domain, linear constraint, differentiable function, continuous symmetric matrix field, directional second-derivative identity, and stationarity in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: the segment between two points of a convex set stays in that set.

[L1] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the Euclidean norm is $\|h\|_2=\sqrt{\langle h,h\rangle}$.

[L2] [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]] and [[def-metric-topology]]: $A$ is continuous and $T=A^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed.

[L3] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: every closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is compact.

[L4] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum.

[L5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: if a real function is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable inside it, some interior derivative equals its endpoint secant slope.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $h_0\in T$ and $Q_{x_*}(h_0)<0$. Set $\phi(t)=f(x_*+th_0)$ for $t$ near $0$. Openness of $U$ permits this definition; stationarity gives $\phi'(0)=0$. The identity in the Statement gives $\phi''(t)=Q_{x_*+th_0}(h_0)$ wherever defined, and continuity of the entries of $H$ makes this negative for every sufficiently small $t\ge0$. [given, L1, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $T\ne\{0\}$ and $Q_{x_*}(h)>0$ for each nonzero $h\in T$. The unit sphere $S_T=\{h\in T:\|h\|_2=1\}$ is nonempty, closed by [L2] and continuity of the norm, and bounded; [L3] makes it compact. The quadratic polynomial $h\mapsto h^{\mathsf T}H(x_*)h$ is continuous, so [L4] gives $\lambda=\min_{h\in S_T}Q_{x_*}(h)>0$. [L1, L2, L3, L4, given]

2.1 Choose such a small $t>0$. Applying [L5] to $\phi'$ on $[0,t]$ gives $\phi'(t)-\phi'(0)=t\phi''(s)<0$ for some $s\in(0,t)$, hence $\phi'(t)<0$; the same argument applies to every positive endpoint up to $t$. Applying [L5] to $\phi$ on $[0,t]$ gives $\phi(t)-\phi(0)=t\phi'(r)<0$ for some $r\in(0,t)$. Since $h_0\in\ker A$, $x_*+th_0$ is feasible, so $x_*$ is not a local minimum. [L5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 By continuity of the finitely many entries of $H$, choose $\delta>0$ so that $\|x-x_*\|_2<\delta$ implies $|Q_x(h)-Q_{x_*}(h)|<\lambda/2$ for every unit vector $h$: expand the difference as a finite sum of entry differences times $h_i h_j$, each with $|h_i h_j|\le1$. If $y\ne x_*$ is feasible and $\|y-x_*\|_2<\delta$, put $v=y-x_*$. Then $v\in T$, and convexity of $U$ keeps $x_*+tv$ in $U$ for $0\le t\le1$. For $\phi(t)=f(x_*+tv)$, stationarity gives $\phi'(0)=0$, while homogeneity of the quadratic form gives $\phi''(t)=Q_{x_*+tv}(v)\ge(\lambda/2)\|v\|_2^2>0$. [F1, L1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 For any $t\in(0,1]$, [L5] applied to $\phi'$ on $[0,t]$ yields $\phi'(t)-\phi'(0)=t\phi''(s)>0$ for some $s\in(0,t)$, so $\phi'(t)>0$. Applying [L5] to $\phi$ on $[0,1]$ gives $\phi(1)-\phi(0)=\phi'(r)>0$ for some $r\in(0,1)$. Thus every distinct feasible $y$ with $\|y-x_*\|_2<\delta$ has $f(y)>f(x_*)$. If $T=\{0\}$, $Ay=Ax_*$ implies $y-x_*\in T=\{0\}$, so $x_*$ is the only feasible point. [L5, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the construction in [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]], $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling; $V_F$ is a real vector space and its displayed operations are representative-independent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The decorated cost algebra, type composition and scaling, and the formal pair relation in the Definition.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]]: types are identified at zero cost in both directions, and a pair difference is identified after adding a common catalyst type.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-decorated-cost-algebra]]: costs satisfy nonnegative closed-cycle bounds, triangle inequalities, translation invariance, and positive homogeneity.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: reversible splitting and recombination are allowed for every positive scaled amount.

## Proof

1.1 The relation $\approx_0$ is reflexive because $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, and symmetric by definition. Suppose $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma'\approx_0\Gamma''$. The triangle inequality gives both directed costs between $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma''$ at most zero. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose a finite reverse witness of cost $d<\epsilon$; such witnesses exist because the reverse infimum is zero. Every forward witness of cost $c$ closes with it, so [F2] gives $c+d\ge0$, hence $c>-\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows every forward witness has nonnegative cost and its infimum is at least zero; the same argument reverses the direction. Both infima are therefore zero, proving transitivity. The same argument proves product compatibility: subadditivity makes both product costs at most zero, and any finite reverse witness bounds every forward product witness below by a quantity tending to zero. Positive homogeneity gives scaling compatibility directly. Thus $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling, and the quotient is a commutative monoid. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Reversible splitting [A1] gives accessible transitions in both directions between $(s+t)\Gamma$ and $s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. Extensivity makes each such edge have zero entropy cost. Any reverse witness bounds all forward costs below by [F2]'s closed-cycle inequality, so both infima are zero. Hence $(s+t)\Gamma\approx_0 s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. The empty type $1$ is an identity under composition; its reassociation and permutation identifications have zero cost by the type conventions. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 The pair relation $\equiv$ is reflexive using unit catalyst $1$ and symmetric by swapping the two sides. Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via catalyst $C$, and $(A',B')\equiv(A'',B'')$ via catalyst $D$. Their witnesses are
$A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C,\qquad
A'\times B''\times D\approx_0 A''\times B'\times D.$
Multiply the first equivalence by $B''\times D$, the second by $B\times C$, and compose. Reassociating and permuting gives
$A\times B''\times(B'\times C\times D)\approx_0 A''\times B\times(B'\times C\times D),$
which witnesses $(A,B)\equiv(A'',B'')$. Hence $\equiv$ is an equivalence relation. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via $C$, so $A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C$. For an arbitrary pair $(D,E)$, multiply this witness by $D\times E$. Reassociation gives $(A\times D)\times(B'\times E)\times C\approx_0(A'\times D)\times(B\times E)\times C$, exactly the witness for $(A\times D,B\times E)\equiv(A'\times D,B'\times E)$. Apply the same argument to a change of representative of $(D,E)$ and use transitivity; addition is representative-independent. Scaling a catalyst witness by $t>0$ and using product compatibility from step 1.1 proves that positive scalar multiplication is representative-independent. Product commutativity and associativity give the additive laws, and the empty type gives $(A\times1,B\times1)=(A,B)$. Swapping a pair gives an inverse: its sum with $(A,B)$ is $(A\times B,B\times A)$, equivalent to $(1,1)$ with unit catalyst because the two product types agree up to permutation and have zero cost in both directions. Thus the classes form an abelian group with zero $[(1,1)]$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 For $t>0$, the displayed operation $t(A,B)=(tA,tB)$ satisfies $t(v+w)=tv+tw$ because scaling distributes over type composition, and $t(sv)=(ts)v$ for $s>0$ by associativity of type scaling. Also $1v=v$. The scalar-addition law for positive $s,t$ follows from step 1.2:
$(s+t)[A,B]=[(s+t)A,(s+t)B]=[sA\times tA,sB\times tB]=s[A,B]+t[A,B].$
The zero scalar is defined as the additive identity, and $(-t)v$ is defined as $t(-v)$, where $-v$ swaps the pair. [F1, step 1.2, step 3.1]

5.1 The positive scalar laws extend to negative scalars by swapping pairs. For the scalar-addition law with opposite signs, write $s-t$ with $s,t\ge0$. If $s\ge t$, positive scalar addition gives $sv=(s-t)v+tv$, so cancellation in the additive group gives $(s-t)v=sv-tv$; if $t>s$, apply the same identity to $t=(t-s)+s$ and negate. Cases with zero are immediate. For scalar composition, write each nonzero scalar as its sign times a positive magnitude; the defined action swaps the pair once for each negative sign and scales by the product of magnitudes, so $(rs)v=r(sv)$, with zero cases immediate. For distributivity over vector addition, positive scalars distribute by step 4.1 and a negative scalar distributes by taking the additive inverse of that identity. Together with the abelian-group laws in step 3.1, these are all real-vector-space axioms. [F1, step 4.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the diagonal model [[def-tdmath-diagonal-operator-model]], the operator $H_E$ is densely defined and self-adjoint on $\ell^2(I)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-diagonal-operator-model]]: $H_E$ has domain $\{x:\sum_i|E_ix_i|^2<\infty\}$ and acts coordinatewise by multiplication by the real numbers $E_i$.

[F2] [[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]: the adjoint domain consists of those $y$ for which $x\mapsto\langle H_Ex,y\rangle$ on $D(H_E)$ is represented by inner product with a vector of $\ell^2(I)$.

[F3] [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]] and [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: square summability is the finite-subset sum condition, and the inner product is linear in the first argument.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$.

## Proof

**Given:** The diagonal operator of [[def-tdmath-diagonal-operator-model]] with real entries $E_i$.

1.1 Every finitely supported sequence belongs to $D(H_E)$. For $x\in\ell^2(I)$, the tails of its square-sum can be made arbitrarily small, so finite-coordinate truncations converge in norm to $x$; finite-support vectors are therefore dense in $\ell^2(I)$. [F1, F3, F4]

1.2 For $x,y\in D(H_E)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] makes $\sum_i|E_ix_i\overline{y_i}|$ finite, and reality of $E_i$ gives $\langle H_Ex,y\rangle=\sum_iE_ix_i\overline{y_i}=\langle x,H_Ey\rangle$. Thus $H_E$ is symmetric. [F1, F3]

2.1 If $y\in D(H_E^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2(I)$ such that $\langle H_Ex,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in D(H_E)$. Taking $x=u_i$ gives $E_i\overline{y_i}=\overline{z_i}$, hence $z_i=E_iy_i$ for every $i$; since $z\in\ell^2(I)$, $y\in D(H_E)$ and $H_E^*y=H_Ey$. Conversely symmetry in step 1.2 shows every $y\in D(H_E)$ is in $D(H_E^*)$ with that value. Therefore $D(H_E^*)=D(H_E)$ and $H_E^*=H_E$. [F1, F2, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** A measure space, its nonnegative integral, and a pointwise increasing measurable sequence.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: nonnegative integrals are suprema over measurable simple minorants; monotonicity follows by inclusion of the minorant sets.

[F2] [[def-finite-sum]]: finite sums of simple-function level values can be regrouped.

[F3] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: bounded nonempty subsets of $\mathbb R$ have suprema.

[A1] Countable additivity of $\mu$ is part of the measure-space definition.

[A2] The sequence is measurable and satisfies $0\le f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise.

## Proof

**Given:** A measure space and a pointwise increasing sequence $0\le f_n\uparrow f$.

1.1 The simple minorants of $f_n$ are also minorants of $f_{n+1}$, so their integral suprema increase. Each is at most $\int f$; hence $L:=\lim_n\int f_n$ exists in $[0,\infty]$ and $L\le\int f$. [F1, A2]

2.1 Fix a nonnegative simple $s\le f$ and $0<t<1$. The measurable sets $A_n:=\{f_n\ge ts\}$ increase and cover $\{s>0\}$, since $f_n(x)\to f(x)\ge s(x)>ts(x)$ there. Write $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$ in disjoint level form. For each $c_j>0$, $A_n\cap B_j\uparrow B_j$; countable additivity, applied to successive disjoint differences, gives $\mu(A_n\cap B_j)\uparrow\mu(B_j)$. The finite-sum definition [F2] then gives $\int s\mathbf1_{A_n}\uparrow\int s$. As $f_n\ge ts\mathbf1_{A_n}$, monotonicity and homogeneity of the simple integral imply $L\ge t\int s$. Let $t\uparrow1$ and take the supremum over $s\le f$; [F1, F3] give $L\ge\int f$. Together with step 1.1 this proves monotone convergence. [F1, F2, F3, A1, A2, step 1.1]

2.2 For nonnegative measurable $f$, define $s_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{f\ge k2^{-n}\}}$. Each $s_n$ is a finite-valued measurable simple function. Every threshold counted in $s_n$ is also counted at the even-index threshold in $s_{n+1}$, so $s_n\le s_{n+1}$. If $f(x)<\infty$, once $n>f(x)$ the mesh gives $0\le f(x)-s_n(x)<2^{-n}$; if $f(x)=\infty$, then $s_n(x)=n$. Thus $s_n\uparrow f$. Define $t_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{g\ge k2^{-n}\}}$; the same threshold and mesh argument shows $t_n\uparrow g$. Apply step 1.1 to $s_n$, $t_n$, and $s_n+t_n$. Refine their finitely many level sets to the finite partition of intersections $B_j\cap C_k$; regrouping the resulting sums by [F2] gives $\int(s_n+t_n)=\int s_n+\int t_n$. Passing to the three monotone limits proves $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$. [F1, F2, A1, step 1.1]

3.1 For $c>0$, simple minorants of $cf$ are exactly $c$ times simple minorants of $f$, so the supremum definition gives $\int cf=c\int f$; for $c=0$ both sides are zero. If an integrable real function is expressed as $u-v$ with $u,v\ge0$ integrable, the value $\int u-\int v$ is independent of the expression: $u-v=u'-v'$ implies $u+v'=u'+v$, and step 2.2 equates the finite sums of integrals. The definition using positive and negative parts is one such expression, so signed integrals are linear. [F1, F2, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: nonnegative integrals are monotone and the integral of a nonnegative measurable function is defined by simple minorants.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence]]: integrals commute with increasing pointwise limits, including infinite values.

[A1] The sequence $f_n$ is nonnegative and measurable on the stated measure space.

## Proof

**Given:** A measure space and measurable $f_n\ge0$.

1.1 Set $h_k:=\inf_{n\ge k}f_n$. For each real $a$, $\{h_k<a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge k}\{f_n<a\}$, so $h_k$ is measurable by the sigma-algebra closure in [F1]. The sequence $h_k$ is increasing and its pointwise limit is $\liminf_n f_n$, which is measurable since $\{\lim_kh_k>a\}=\bigcup_k\{h_k>a\}$. [F1, A1]

2.1 For every $n\ge k$, monotonicity gives $\int h_k\le\int f_n$, so $\int h_k\le\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n$. Taking $k\to\infty$ and applying monotone convergence to $h_k$ yields $\int\liminf f_n=\lim_k\int h_k\le\lim_k\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n=\liminf_n\int f_n$. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let a finite canonical model have energies $E_i$, ground energy $E_0$, and exactly $g\ge1$ states at $E_0$, with every other energy strictly larger. As $\beta\to+\infty$, each ground-state probability tends to $1/g$, each excited-state probability tends to zero, and the Shannon entropy $-\sum_i p_i(\beta)\log p_i(\beta)$ tends to $\log g$. This is a finite-model statement only.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] The state set is finite and nonempty, $E_0=\min_iE_i$, exactly $g$ states attain it, and every remaining gap $E_i-E_0$ is positive.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: finite canonical weights are $p_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ and Shannon entropy uses natural logarithms.

[F2] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: exponential is positive; logarithms convert products to sums and are continuous on positive reals.

[F3] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: $\beta e^{-\beta\Delta}\to0$ for every fixed $\Delta>0$.

## Proof

**Given:** A finite energy list with ground energy $E_0$, degeneracy $g\ge1$, and positive gaps for all other states.

1.1 Factor $e^{-\beta E_0}$ from the partition sum to obtain $Z=e^{-\beta E_0}(g+\sum_{i:E_i>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_i-E_0)})$. Every gap is positive, and there are finitely many, so the parenthesized sum tends to $g$. Thus each ground probability tends to $1/g$ and every excited probability tends to zero. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Ground-state entropy terms tend to $-g(1/g)\log(1/g)=\log g$. For an excited state with gap $\Delta_i>0$, step 1.1 gives $p_i=O(e^{-\beta\Delta_i})$ and $\log p_i=-\beta\Delta_i-\log D(\beta)$, where $D(\beta):=g+\sum_{j:E_j>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_j-E_0)}\to g>0$ by step 1.1, so $\log D(\beta)$ is bounded by continuity of $\log$; hence $|p_i\log p_i|=O((1+\beta)e^{-\beta\Delta_i})\to0$ by [F3]. The excited sum is finite, so its limit is zero and the total entropy tends to $\log g$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^m$, an open $U$, a vector field with continuous first partial derivatives, and $q_0\in U$.

[F1] [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]: continuous partial derivatives on an open neighborhood imply total differentiability there, with derivative the Jacobian.

[F2] [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]: on a convex open set, a uniform bound on the derivative operator norm gives the corresponding Lipschitz bound.

[F3] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: every continuous real component on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

[F4] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: if a continuous function on a closed interval has a Riemann-integrable interior derivative, its integral is the endpoint increment.

## Proof

**Given:** $U,X,q_0$ as in the Statement; use the componentwise Riemann integral for continuous $\mathbb R^m$-valued functions.

1.1 By openness choose $R>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,2R)\subset U$. Continuity of $X$ and $DX$ at $q_0$ gives finite $M,L\ge0$ bounding $\|X\|$ on $\overline B(q_0,R)$ and $\|DX\|$ on $B(q_0,2R)$. By [F1] $X$ is totally differentiable there, and [F2] applied to the convex ball $B(q_0,2R)$ gives $\|X(u)-X(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|$ for $u,v\in\overline B(q_0,R)$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Let $\mathcal C$ be the closed ball in $C([-\delta,\delta],\mathbb R^m)$ of curves with values in $\overline B(q_0,R)$, with the supremum norm. It is complete: a Cauchy sequence converges uniformly componentwise because $\mathbb R^m$ is complete; its uniform limit is continuous and remains in the closed ball. For $p\in\overline B(q_0,R/2)$ define $T_p\gamma(t):=p+\int_0^t X(\gamma(s))\,ds$. The integrand is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. Choose $\delta>0$ with $M\delta\le R/2$ and $L\delta<1$. Then $T_p$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, since $\|T_p\gamma(t)-q_0\|\le\|p-q_0\|+M|t|\le R$, and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, construct]

3.1 Starting at the constant curve $\gamma_0(t)=p$, iterate $\gamma_{k+1}=T_p\gamma_k$. If $\kappa=L\delta<1$, then $\|\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_k\|_\infty\le\kappa^k\|\gamma_1-\gamma_0\|_\infty$; the geometric tail bound makes $(\gamma_k)$ uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $\phi(\cdot,p)\in\mathcal C$ is a fixed point by the contraction bound. Any two fixed points have distance at most $\kappa$ times that distance, so they coincide. [step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 For $g(s)=X(\phi(s,p))$, continuity and [F3] make every component Riemann integrable. At an interior $t$, the difference quotient of $\phi(t,p)=p+\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ differs from $g(t)$ by at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|$, which tends to zero by continuity; thus $\partial_t\phi=X(\phi)$. Conversely any $C^1$ solution staying in the ball satisfies the fixed-point equation by [F4], so uniqueness of the fixed point is uniqueness of the IVP. [step 3.1, F3, F4]

4.2 If $p,p'$ lie in $\overline B(q_0,R/2)$, subtract their fixed-point equations from step 3.1 and take suprema to obtain $\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty\le\|p-p'\|+L\delta\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty$. Since $L\delta<1$, division gives the local Lipschitz estimate $(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|p-p'\|$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, algebra]

5.1 Whenever the compositions remain in the chosen ball, both $t\mapsto\phi(t+s,p)$ and $t\mapsto\phi(t,\phi(s,p))$ solve the same IVP at $t=0$, with initial value $\phi(s,p)$. Uniqueness from step 4.1 gives the local flow law; setting $t=-s$ gives the local inverse relation. [step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated Euclidean domains, $C^2$ regularity, and the local contraction flow of [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]].

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]]: a continuous-derivative vector field has a unique local flow, a Volterra integral equation, locally Lipschitz dependence on initial data, and the local flow law.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable maps, $D(g\circ f)=Dg\circ Df$ at the corresponding point.

[F3] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: continuous coefficient functions are integrable on compact intervals, and an integrable interior derivative evaluates by its endpoint increment.

[F4] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] and [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]: a closed bounded Euclidean ball is compact, and continuous finite-dimensional derivative fields on it are uniformly continuous.

## Proof

**Given:** Choose a compact closed ball $K$ inside the field domain and a time interval $[-\delta,\delta]$ so all flow points and line segments used below remain in $K$. By [F4], $K$ is compact; continuity of $DX$ and $D^2X$ makes $L:=\sup_K\|DX\|$ and $M_2:=\sup_K\|D^2X\|$ finite. Shrink $\delta$ so $L\delta<1$. Matrix and tensor norms are Euclidean operator norms; vector-valued integrals are componentwise Riemann integrals.

1.1 For $p$ near $q$ put $\Delta_h(t):=\phi_X^t(p+h)-\phi_X^t(p)$. The integral equations from [F1] and the one-variable fundamental theorem applied to $\theta\mapsto X(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))$ give
$$\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_0^t A_h(s)\Delta_h(s)\,ds,\quad A_h(s):=\int_0^1DX(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))\,d\theta.$$
The segments lie in $K$ after shrinking the initial ball and time interval. The local Lipschitz estimate in [F1] gives $\sup_t\|\Delta_h(t)\|=O(\|h\|)$. Uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$ from [F4] makes $A_h(s)$ converge uniformly to $DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ as $h\to0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 The linear integral equation $J(t)=I+\int_0^tDX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s)\,ds$ has a unique continuous solution: on the complete space $C([ -\delta,\delta],M_m(\mathbb R))$, the map $T(J)(t)=I+\int_0^tDX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s)\,ds$ has contraction constant at most $L\delta$. Its closed ball of radius $(1-L\delta)^{-1}$ maps into itself because $1+L\delta(1-L\delta)^{-1}=(1-L\delta)^{-1}$; the contraction iteration therefore converges uniformly to its unique fixed point. Define $R_h(t):=\Delta_h(t)-J(t)h$. Subtracting the integral equations and writing the integrand difference as $(A_h-DX(\phi_X^s(p)))\Delta_h+DX(\phi_X^s(p))R_h$ gives
$$\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+\delta\|A_h-DX(\phi_X^s(p))\|_\infty\|\Delta_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|).$$
Thus $D_q\phi_X^t(p)=J(t,p)$. The continuous integrand in the equation for $J$ has average over $[t,t+h]$ tending to its value at $t$: the quotient error is at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|DX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s,p)-DX(\phi_X^t(p))J(t,p)\|$, which tends to zero. Thus $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(p))J$ and $J(0,p)=I$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 Write $J_h(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $J_0(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p)$. Subtracting their integral equations gives
$$J_h-J_0=\int_0^t DX(\phi_h)(J_h-J_0)\,ds+\int_0^t(DX(\phi_h)-DX(\phi_0))J_0\,ds,$$
where $\phi_h=\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $\phi_0=\phi_X^s(p)$. Boundedness of $D^2X$ on $K$ and $\phi_h-\phi_0=O(\|h\|)$ bound the second integral by $C\|h\|$ for a fixed $C$; the first integral has norm at most $L\delta\|J_h-J_0\|_\infty$. Since $L\delta<1$, absorption gives $J_h-J_0=O(\|h\|)$ uniformly in time. Uniform continuity of $D^2X$ on $K$ and the integral mean-value formula give, uniformly in $s$,
$$DX(\phi_h)-DX(\phi_0)=D^2X(\phi_0)[\phi_h-\phi_0,\cdot]+o(\|h\|)=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|),$$
using $\phi_h-\phi_0=J_0h+o(\|h\|)$ from step 2.1. Also $J_h=J_0+O(\|h\|)$. Substitute these expansions in the subtracted equation: the forcing term is
$$\int_0^tD^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,J_0(\cdot)]\,ds+o(\|h\|),$$
uniformly in time. For each $h$, let $K_h$ solve the linear integral equation obtained by retaining this displayed leading term and the coefficient $DX(\phi_0)$; existence and uniqueness follow from the same contraction bound $L\delta<1$. Then $R_h:=J_h-J_0-K_h$ satisfies $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+o(\|h\|)$, so $R_h=o(\|h\|)$. Thus $D_pJ[h](v)=K_h(v)$, and, writing $K_2[u,v]=D_q^2\phi_X[u,v]$, it is the unique solution
$$K_2(t)[u,v]=\int_0^t\big(DX(\phi_X^s)K_2(s)[u,v]+D^2X(\phi_X^s)[J(s)u,J(s)v]\big)\,ds.$$
The integral equation makes $K_2$ bilinear in $(u,v)$; the same contraction estimate and continuity of its coefficients give continuous dependence on $(t,p)$. [step 2.1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

3.2 Let $V(t):=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and $W(t):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)$. By [F2] and the variational equation, $V'=DY(\phi_X^t)X(\phi_X^t)$ and $W'=DX(\phi_X^t)W$. The identity $[X,Y]=0$ makes $V$ solve this same linear equation with $V(0)=W(0)=Y(q)$; uniqueness from the contraction argument gives $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$. [F1, F2, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $\partial_t\phi_X=X(\phi_X)$, the chain rule [F2] gives the continuous mixed derivative $\partial_tD_q\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)J$; differentiating in $t$ gives the continuous derivative $\partial_t^2\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)X(\phi_X)$. Steps 2.1 and 2.1 give the continuous first and second derivatives in $q$, so every first- and second-order partial derivative in $(t,q)$ exists and is continuous. Hence the local flow is jointly $C^2$. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 For fixed $t$, the curve $s\mapsto\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ has derivative $D\phi_X^t\,Y(\phi_Y^s(q))=Y(\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ by step 3.2, and starts at $\phi_X^t(q)$. It is therefore the $Y$-flow from that initial point; IVP uniqueness from [F1] yields $\phi_X^t\phi_Y^s(q)=\phi_Y^s\phi_X^t(q)$. [step 3.2, F1, F2] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open, and let $\omega$ be a nowhere-zero $C^2$ one-form, with the horizontal paths of [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]. Assume that every point has a neighborhood $W$ with $S\in C^2(W)$ and nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ satisfying $dS=\mu\omega$. For every $q\in U$, its horizontal reachability class in $U$ is contained in a countable union of compact subsets of $U$ with empty interior. Consequently every nonempty open $V\subseteq U$ contains a point not horizontally reachable from $q$ by any horizontal path in $U$. In particular, if $q\in V$, that point is not reachable by a path contained in $V$. No global first integral or choice axiom is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open Euclidean domain, nowhere-zero $C^2$ form, two-sided finite-piece horizontal paths, and local first integrals in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]: a horizontal path is piecewise $C^1$, with finitely many pieces, and its tangent lies in $\ker\omega$; constant paths, reversal and finite concatenation are admissible.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] and [[lem-tdmath-variational-flow-and-commutation]]: $C^2$ vector fields have unique local $C^2$ flows, available for both time signs, with inverse flow and differentiable dependence.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: composition derivatives obey the chain rule, and a real differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: a $C^1$ zero equation with a specified invertible solved-coordinate minor has a local $C^1$ graph with the displayed derivative formula. Its present batch-4 carrier remains draft; the graph uses here await final native supplier handoff.

[F4] [[thm-connected-subsets-of-r-are-intervals]]: every interval is connected; it cannot be partitioned into two nonempty relatively open sets.

[F5] [[thm-rationals-countable]] and [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]: the rational numbers admit an enumeration and are dense in the reals, without a choice hypothesis. Finite words and finite rational tuples can be enumerated by length and by the sum of their integer indices.

[F6] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]] and [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]: a closed bounded parameter box is compact; its continuous image is compact and closed in the Euclidean ambient space. These suppliers are choice-free.

[F7] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]: every Euclidean Cauchy sequence converges, coordinatewise from real completeness.

[F8] [[thm-recursion]] and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]: a recursively prescribed least natural-number index defines a sequence without arbitrary selections.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use the local first integrals in the Statement. Write $\omega=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\omega_j dx_j$ in the fixed Euclidean coordinates and set $w=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{n+1})$ and $Z_j=e_j-(\omega_j/|w|^2)w$. These globally defined $C^2$ vector fields are horizontal and span $\ker\omega$ at each point, since their matrix is the orthogonal projection onto that kernel. On every neighborhood supplied by the hypothesis, $dS=\mu\omega$ has nonzero derivative, and each $Z_j$-flow preserves $S$ as long as its trajectory remains there, by [F3]. Its derivative therefore preserves horizontal tangent vectors there: differentiating $S(\phi_j^t(x))=S(x)$ gives $dS_{\phi_j^t(x)}D\phi_j^t(x)v=dS_xv=0$ for horizontal $v$. The compact image of any finite flow trajectory has a finite subcover by such neighborhoods; a sufficiently fine finite subdivision of its compact time interval puts each subtrajectory in one of them. This follows directly from compactness: otherwise shrinking subintervals failing the subdivision would have a limiting time whose neighborhood contains them. Composing the local derivative identities obtains preservation over the full duration. Local flow uniqueness makes these continuations consistent, and [F2] gives $C^2$ dependence on durations and initial points wherever the finite composition is defined. [F1, F2, F3, F6, given, construct]

2.1 Fix $q\in U$, and let $\mathcal O(q)$ consist of endpoints of all finite words of the $n+1$ fields $Z_j$, with signed durations and intermediate trajectories in $U$; include the empty word. At any $r$, choose $n$ of these fields forming a basis of $\ker\omega_r$. In a neighborhood from the hypothesis, [L1] applied to $S(x)-S(r)$ gives a local graph plaque with $n$ free coordinates. Composing the $n$ chosen flows for small durations gives endpoints in that plaque. The derivative at zero, followed by projection to the plaque's free coordinates, is invertible, because those vectors form its tangent basis; apply [L1] to this free-coordinate endpoint map minus a target, with durations solved, to see that the endpoints contain a plaque neighborhood of $r$. All these paths stay in the chosen neighborhood. A horizontal piecewise $C^1$ path preserves the local $S$ by [F3], so near every one of its parameter values it lies in this plaque neighborhood and hence in the same finite-word orbit as that point. The finite-word orbits form equivalence classes by reversal and concatenation, and their preimages along the path are consequently relatively open in its interval domain. By [F4], connectedness of that interval forces one class. Thus every point horizontally reachable from $q$ lies in $\mathcal O(q)$; the reverse inclusion follows because each word is a horizontal concatenation. [F1, F2, F3, F4, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For a fixed finite word $\alpha$ of length $m\ge1$, write $F_\alpha:O_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to U$ for its endpoint map from $q$, on the open set of admissible duration tuples. Each duration derivative is a field vector transported by the later flows and is horizontal by step 1.1. Near any $s\in O_\alpha$, continuity puts the endpoint image in a neighborhood with the first integral $S$ from the hypothesis; hence $D(S\circ F_\alpha)=0$. On a small convex parameter ball, [F3] makes $S\circ F_\alpha$ constant. Choose a closed box with rational endpoints, containing $s$ in its interior and contained in that ball. Its image under $F_\alpha$ is compact by [F6], lies in one level of $S$, and has empty interior in $U$: a nonempty open subset of that image would make $S$ constant on an open set, contradicting $dS=\mu\omega\ne0$. Thus the image is a closed nowhere-dense subset of $U$. By [F5], enumerate the countable collection of all finite words and rational closed parameter boxes; for an admissible box whose compact image has empty interior record that image, and otherwise record the empty set. Include the singleton $\{q\}$ for the empty word. This explicitly defined sequence $(K_j)$ of closed nowhere-dense sets covers $\mathcal O(q)$, since every duration tuple admits the small box just constructed. No countable atlas or choice of first integrals is needed for the enumeration. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Let $V$ be any nonempty open subset of $U$. Choose a rational open Euclidean ball with closure contained in $V$. Recursively choose the first ball in a fixed enumeration of rational balls whose closure is inside the preceding open ball, disjoint from $K_j$, and whose radius is below $2^{-j}$. Such a ball exists because $K_j$ is closed with empty interior. If the $j$th ball has center $c_j$ and radius $r_j<2^{-j}$, then all later centers lie in its closed ball, so $|c_k-c_j|\le r_j$ for $k>j$. Thus the centers form a Cauchy sequence; [F7] gives a limit $p$ in all the nested closed balls, hence in $V$ and outside every $K_j$. Each selection is the least natural-number index satisfying explicit nonempty conditions, so it uses no choice axiom. Since the $K_j$ cover $\mathcal O(q)$, step 2.1 shows $p$ is not horizontally reachable from $q$ even by a path in $U$, and therefore not by one in $V$. This proves the asserted conclusion for every nonempty open $V$, using no global first integral or choice axiom. [given, F5, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $v_a,v_b\in\mathbb R$ with $v_a<v_b$. A fraction $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfies $v=(1-\lambda)v_a+\lambda v_b$ exactly when $v\in[v_a,v_b]$ and

$$\lambda=\frac{v-v_a}{v_b-v_a}.$$

This fraction is unique. At $v=v_a$ it is $0$, and at $v=v_b$ it is $1$; no admissible fraction gives a value outside the endpoint interval.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Ordered real numbers $v_a<v_b$, an interval point $v\in\mathbb R$, and a mixing fraction $\lambda\in[0,1]$.

[F1] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: $\mathbb R$ is an ordered field, so division by the positive number $v_b-v_a$ is valid and preserves inequalities.

[F2] [[def-interval]]: $[0,1]=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:0\le\lambda\le1\}$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 From $v=(1-\lambda)v_a+\lambda v_b$ one obtains $v-v_a=\lambda(v_b-v_a)$. Since $v_b-v_a>0$ and $0\le\lambda\le1$, this gives $v_a\le v\le v_b$ and forces $\lambda=(v-v_a)/(v_b-v_a)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, if $v_a\le v\le v_b$, the quotient $\lambda=(v-v_a)/(v_b-v_a)$ lies in $[0,1]$ and substitution gives $v=(1-\lambda)v_a+\lambda v_b$. The same forced quotient proves uniqueness and yields the two endpoint values. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. The nonnegative integral defined by
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] equals the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral
defined by [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], with the same value in
$[0,+\infty]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ and a nonnegative measurable
function $f$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] defines a nonnegative simple integral by
finite sums $\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$, with $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$, and defines
$\int f\,d\mu$ as the supremum over measurable simple minorants
$0\le s\le f$. Its current batch-11 carrier is a draft definition; no proof
is required for this definition-like supplier.

[F2] [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] defines the shared nonnegative
integral as the supremum over the same class of nonnegative simple minorants.

[F3] [[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]] characterizes nonnegative
simple functions as finite-range measurable maps, and
[[def-simple-function-and-canonical-representation]] gives each such function
its finite partition into level sets.

[F4] [[def-measure]] supplies the countably additive measure $\mu$ in the
measure space. [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]] uses the finite sum
$\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$ with the convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$;
[[lem-well-definedness-of-the-simple-integral]] proves that this value does not
depend on the chosen simple representation.

## Proof

1.1 A nonnegative simple function in the thermodynamics definition is a finite
sum of indicators of disjoint measurable sets, hence is measurable and has
finite range; conversely, the level sets in [F3] represent every nonnegative
finite-range measurable function in that form. Thus the two definitions use
the same class of simple minorants. [F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 For any simple minorant $s$, use its canonical level-set representation
from [F3]. Both [F1] and [F4] assign the same finite sum
$\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$ to $s$, including zero coefficients on sets of infinite
measure; [F4] ensures the shared value is representation-independent. Hence
the two definitions assign the same value to every minorant. [F1, F3, F4,
step 1.1]

3.1 The two nonnegative integrals are suprema over the same minorants with the
same value for each minorant by steps 1.1 and 2.1. Their suprema therefore agree,
including when the common value is $+\infty$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]
∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, let $\phi$ be a stable pair
potential as in [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] with
stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. In fixed reference length and
energy units, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L]^d$ and define, for $N\ge1$,
$$Z_{L,N}:=\frac{a^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta U_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N},$$
where $\lambda_d$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R^d$, $\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ is its $N$-fold product measure. The
integrand uses the ordinary real exponential when $U_N<+\infty$ and is defined
to be $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$. Also,
$\int_{\Lambda_L^N}f\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ abbreviates the nonnegative
integral of $f\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$ on the full product space, using
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. Set $Z_{L,0}=1$.
Define $\Xi_L:=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}Z_{L,N}$ as the nonnegative extended sum of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. For $L\ge1$ put
$Q:=a e^{\beta B}$. Choose any real $K>eQ+1$ and set
$$n_L:=\lfloor K L^d\rfloor+1.$$
which satisfies $K L^d<n_L\le K L^d+1$ by the integer-part lemma
[[lem-integer-part]]. Let
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}:=\sum_{N=0}^{n_L}Z_{L,N}$. Then
$$1\le\Xi_L\le e^{Q L^d},\qquad \sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-L^d},\qquad \Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a dimension $d\ge1$, the model in
[[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]], its stability constant
$B$, $a,\beta>0$, and $L\ge1$.

[A1] Stability means $U_N\ge-BN$ for every finite configuration and every
$N\ge1$ ([[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]]).

[L1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] defines the nonnegative integral as the
supremum of simple minorants. This current batch-11 definition is draft text;
its exact interface is inspected in the batch dependency evidence.

[F1] [[def-countable-choice]] states $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the standard
Lebesgue measure and box suppliers used here state this assumption explicitly.

[F2] [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] defines
$\lambda_d$ as Lebesgue measure on its measurable sets; restricting it to
Borel sets gives a measure. [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] gives
$\lambda_d([0,L]^d)=L^d$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$;
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] gives
the rectangle formula for finite products of sigma-finite measures.

[F3] [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]
ensures the Lebesgue factors are sigma-finite, so the finite product measures
in the Definition exist.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] defines
$e^x=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}x^N/N!$, with integer powers as in
[[def-integer-power]]; [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]] proves
convergence for every real $x$.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]] gives $e^xe^y=e^{x+y}$, and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]] gives monotonicity of $e^x$.

[F6] [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] defines $0!=1$ and the ordinary
factorial recursion; [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]] defines the series
sum as the supremum of its nonnegative partial sums, allowing $+\infty$.

[F7] [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] identifies
the finite product Borel sigma-algebra, and extended-real measurability means
measurability of preimages of extended-real Borel sets
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Coordinate-difference maps are
continuous, hence Borel under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]); composition with the Borel
potential preserves measurability
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). Finite
sums of the resulting extended-real measurable terms are measurable whenever
defined ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).
On finite energy values $u$, $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ is continuous; assigning
the value $0$ at $u=+\infty$ remains Borel because $\{+\infty\}$ is Borel
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]). The box indicator is measurable,
so the integrand extended by zero off $\Lambda_L^N$ is product-measurable.

[F8] [[lem-integer-part]] gives, for every real $x$, an integer
$\lfloor x\rfloor$ with $\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1$.

## Proof

1.1 By [A1] and $\beta>0$, every configuration satisfies
$0\le e^{-\beta U_N}\le e^{\beta BN}$, with the value $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$.
Fact [F7] makes the integrand and its restriction to $\Lambda_L^N$
measurable. For every simple minorant of this restricted integrand, [L1]
bounds its integral by the integral of the constant $e^{\beta BN}$ on
$\Lambda_L^N$. [A1, F1, F7, L1, algebra]

2.1 The box and product-measure formulas [F2, F3] give
$\lambda_d^{\otimes N}(\Lambda_L^N)=L^{dN}$. Thus
$Z_{L,N}\le(ae^{\beta B}L^d)^N/N!=(QL^d)^N/N!$ for $N\ge1$, and this
also holds for $N=0$ since $Z_{L,0}=1$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Summing the nonnegative terms by [F6] and using [F4] gives
$1\le\Xi_L\le\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}(QL^d)^N/N!=e^{QL^d}$; the lower bound is
the empty-configuration term. [F4, F6, step 2.1]

3.2 By [F8], $KL^d<n_L\le KL^d+1$. If $N>n_L$, then $N>KL^d$, so
$1\le e^{N-KL^d}$. Therefore
$$\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N>n_L}\frac{(eQL^d)^N}{N!}\le e^{-KL^d}e^{eQL^d}=e^{(eQ-K)L^d}\le e^{-L^d}.$$
The second inequality extends a nonnegative partial tail to the full
exponential series; the equality uses [F5], and the last inequality follows
from $K>eQ+1$ and [F5]. [F4, F5, F8, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each $M>n_L$, split the $M$th partial sum into the fixed finite prefix
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}$ and the finite tail from $n_L+1$ through $M$.
Taking suprema over $M$ in the nonnegative-series definition [F6] gives
$\Xi_L=\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}+\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}$; subtraction is valid because
step 3.1 proves $\Xi_L<\infty$. Since $\Xi_L\ge1$, step 3.2 implies
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\Xi_L-e^{-L^d}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L$.
[F6, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\phi$ be power-tempered as in
[[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]], with constants
$C,R,\epsilon>0$. Define
$$S_{d,\epsilon}:=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\bigl((2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\bigr)m^{-d-\epsilon},\qquad \|k\|_\infty:=\max_{1\le r\le d}|k_r| \quad(k\in\mathbb Z^d).$$
This nonnegative series, defined by [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]],
groups the lattice terms by shells $\|k\|_\infty=m$.
Then $S_{d,\epsilon}<\infty$. Let $\ell>0$, $g\ge R$, and let
$J\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be finite with $M=|J|$. For each $j\in J$, place at most
$n$ particles in the cube $C_j=(\ell+g)j+[0,\ell]^d$, where $n$ is a
nonnegative integer. The total absolute inter-cube energy satisfies
$$\sum_{\substack{j,j'\in J\;j<j'}}\;\sum_{q\in C_j}\sum_{q'\in C_{j'}}|\phi(q-q')|\le\frac C2 M n^2 S_{d,\epsilon}g^{-d-\epsilon}.$$
Here $j<j'$ means any fixed total ordering of the finite set $J$; each
unordered pair of cubes is counted once.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $d\ge1$, power-tempering constants $C,R,\epsilon>0$, $\ell>0$,
$g\ge R$, a finite index set $J\subset\mathbb Z^d$, and at most $n$ particles
in each translated cube $C_j$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]]: for
$\|x\|_2\ge R$, $|\phi(x)|\le C\|x\|_2^{-d-\epsilon}$.

[F2] [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]] defines a nonnegative series as the
supremum of its partial sums; [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] proves
$\sum_{m\ge1}m^{-p}<\infty$ for every real $p>1$.

[F3] [[def-integers]] supplies the integer lattice. For an integer $m\ge1$,
the lattice box
$\{k:\|k\|_\infty\le m\}$ has $(2m+1)^d$ points because each of the
$d$ coordinates has $2m+1$ independent choices. Subtracting the box of radius
$m-1$ gives shell count $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $m=\|j-j'\|_\infty\ge1$ for two distinct cube indices. In a coordinate
where the index difference is $m$, the nearest points of the two intervals are
separated by $m(\ell+g)-\ell=(m-1)\ell+mg\ge mg$. Hence every pair of points
in $C_j,C_{j'}$ has Euclidean distance at least $mg$. [given, algebra]

1.2 For $m\ge1$, [F3] gives the shell count. Use
$x^d-y^d=(x-y)\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}x^{d-1-r}y^r$ with $x=2m+1$, $y=2m-1$.
Since $2m+1\le3m$, it yields
$$ (2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\le2d(3m)^{d-1}=2d3^{d-1}m^{d-1}. $$
Therefore $S_{d,\epsilon}\le2d3^{d-1}\sum_{m\ge1}m^{-1-\epsilon}<\infty$ by
[F2], since $1+\epsilon>1$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and step 1.1, each such pair contributes at most
$C(mg)^{-d-\epsilon}$ in absolute value, because $mg\ge g\ge R$ and the
Euclidean norm dominates the absolute value of any coordinate. [F1, step 1.1,
algebra]

3.1 For a fixed cube $C_j$, sum step 2.1 over all other indices in $J$ and
enlarge the finite set of index differences to all nonzero lattice vectors.
By [F3], grouping these vectors by $m=\|k\|_\infty$ gives exactly the series
$S_{d,\epsilon}$ of the Statement, whose nonnegative sum is defined by [F2].
the result is at most $Cn^2S_{d,\epsilon}g^{-d-\epsilon}$. Summing this bound
over the $M$ cubes counts each unordered pair twice, so dividing by $2$ gives
the claimed inequality. [F2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

self-adjoint $h$ from [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let
$\lambda_0\le\lambda_1\le\cdots$ be its eigenvalues repeated with
multiplicity, and let $\psi_k$ be a corresponding orthonormal eigenbasis. For

$$\rho_{\beta,M}f:=\sum_{k=0}^M e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$

$$\rho_\beta f:=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$

$$\epsilon_{\mathbf n}=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\alpha_j, \qquad\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N.$$

$$Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, finite data $N,a_j,c,C_0,V$, the form domain $Q$, and $\beta>0$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: countable eigenbasis choices are permitted.

[F4] [[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]]: under Countable Choice, a compact bounded operator that is the operator-norm limit of rank-one partial sums $\sum_{k\le M}\langle\cdot,u_k\rangle v_k$ with $\sum_k\|u_k\|\|v_k\|<\infty$ is trace class, with trace norm at most that coefficient sum.

[F5] [[thm-trace-of-a-positive-operator-is-the-sum-of-its-eigenvalues]]: for a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator the trace is the sum of its eigenvalues with multiplicity.

[F6] [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]: every bounded linear functional on a complex Hilbert space is represented by a unique inner-product vector, with representing-vector norm equal to the functional norm.

[F7] [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]: a trace-class operator has an absolutely convergent basis trace, equal to the trace computed from any nuclear representation.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $N\ge1$, $a_j,c>0$, $V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0$, the interacting form, and $\beta>0$.

1.1 Each $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$ is finite, and only finitely many multi-indices have $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\le M$ for any real $M$: for $M\ge0$, that inequality bounds every nonnegative integer $n_j$ by $M/(2\alpha_j)$, while for $M<0$ there are none. Fix the explicit degree-then-lexicographic enumeration of $\mathbb N_0^N$. Recursively, among the remaining tuples choose one of least energy, breaking a tie by that fixed enumeration; such a least energy exists because below the energy of the first remaining tuple there are only finitely many candidates. Every tuple is eventually listed, since only finitely many tuples have energy at most its energy. This gives the nondecreasing list $(\epsilon_k)_{k\ge0}$ with multiplicity. [F2, algebra]

1.2 On $C_c^\infty$, the shifted interacting form has weight $V+C_0+2\ge c|q|^2+2$, so it dominates the shifted oscillator form from [F2]. Therefore a Cauchy sequence in $Q$ is Cauchy in the oscillator form norm; the identity map extends to a continuous map $Q\to Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, with the same $L^2$ representative because both completions inject into $H_N$ by [F3]. Subtracting the shifts in the two form norms gives
$$q_h(u)=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2\ge q_{\mathrm{osc}}(u)-C_0\|u\|_2^2\qquad(u\in Q).$$
[F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Fix $k\ge0$ and let $L_k=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_0,\ldots,\psi_k\}$. The linear map from $L_k$ to the span of the first $k$ oscillator eigenvectors, sending $u$ to its $k$ oscillator coefficients, has a nonzero kernel because $\dim L_k=k+1>k$. Choose $u\ne0$ in that kernel. Since $u$ lies in the span of the first $k+1$ interacting eigenvectors, [F1] gives $q_h(u)\le\lambda_k\|u\|_2^2$. Its oscillator coefficients at indices below $k$ vanish, so [F2] gives $q_{\mathrm{osc}}(u)\ge\epsilon_k\|u\|_2^2$. Step 1.2 now yields $\lambda_k\|u\|_2^2\ge q_h(u)\ge(\epsilon_k-C_0)\|u\|_2^2$, hence
$$\lambda_k\ge\epsilon_k-C_0.$$
This argument also covers $k=0$, when the span of zero oscillator vectors is $\{0\}$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1 and $\beta>0$,
$$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k} \le e^{\beta C_0}\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N} e^{-\beta\epsilon_{\mathbf n}} =e^{\beta C_0}\prod_{j=1}^N \left(\sum_{n_j\ge0}e^{-\beta(2n_j+1)\alpha_j}\right) =e^{\beta C_0}\prod_{j=1}^N \frac{e^{-\beta\alpha_j}}{1-e^{-2\beta\alpha_j}}.$$
The factorization follows first for finite rectangular sums by distributivity and then by increasing limits of nonnegative sums. Each denominator is positive because $0<e^{-2\beta\alpha_j}<1$. The lower bound $Z_\beta>0$ follows from its positive ground term. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The coefficients satisfy $0<e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\le e^{\beta C_0}$ by [F1]. For each $f$, Parseval makes the finite partial sums in the defining series for $\rho_\beta f$ Cauchy in $H_N$, so the series converges; its coefficient formula gives linearity and $\|\rho_\beta f\|_2\le e^{\beta C_0}\|f\|_2$. Moreover Parseval gives
$$\|\rho_\beta-\rho_{\beta,M}\|\le\sup_{k>M}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\longrightarrow0,$$
since $\lambda_k\to+\infty$ and $\beta>0$. Each truncation is finite rank and hence compact by [F10], so the operator-norm limit $\rho_\beta$ is compact by [F11]. The same convergence makes its rank-one partial sums converge in operator norm, and their coefficient sum is $\sum_ke^{-\beta\lambda_k}=Z_\beta<\infty$; thus $\rho_\beta$ is trace class by [F4]. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F10, F11, F12, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since each $e^{-\beta\lambda_k}$ is real, the Fourier expansion [F12] gives
$$\langle\rho_\beta f,g\rangle=\sum_k e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k,g\rangle=\langle f,\rho_\beta g\rangle$$
for all $f,g\in H_N$; the series is absolutely convergent by Cauchy--Schwarz
for the coefficient sequences and boundedness of the weights. Thus
$\rho_\beta$ is self-adjoint. It is positive because
$$\langle\rho_\beta f,f\rangle =\sum_ke^{-\beta\lambda_k}|\langle f,\psi_k\rangle|^2\ge0.$$
The defining series gives $\rho_\beta\psi_k=e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\psi_k$. If $\rho_\beta x=\mu x$, taking Fourier coefficients shows $(e^{-\beta\lambda_k}-\mu)\langle x,\psi_k\rangle=0$ for every $k$. Completeness [F1, F12] then implies that every nonzero eigenspace is exactly the span of basis vectors with the corresponding repeated diagonal value; since every diagonal value is positive, $0$ is not an eigenvalue. Thus the eigenvalues with multiplicity are precisely $(e^{-\beta\lambda_k})$, and [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta)=Z_\beta$. For bounded $B$, each $\rho_{\beta,M}B$ is finite rank and hence compact by [F10], while
$$\|\rho_{\beta,M}B-\rho_\beta B\|\le\|\rho_{\beta,M}-\rho_\beta\|\,\|B\|\to0$$
by step 4.1. Therefore $\rho_\beta B$ is compact by [F11]. The functional $x\mapsto\langle Bx,\psi_k\rangle$ is linear and has norm at most $\|B\|$ by [F9] and [F8]. By [F6] it is represented by a vector $w_k$ with $\|w_k\|\le\|B\|$ and $\langle Bx,\psi_k\rangle=\langle x,w_k\rangle$. Hence
$$\rho_\beta Bx=\sum_k\langle x,w_k\rangle e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\psi_k.$$
The partial sums converge in operator norm: the norm of the tail after $M$ is at most $\|B\|\sum_{k>M}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\to0$ by step 3.1. This nuclear representation has coefficient sum at most $\|B\|Z_\beta$. Since $\rho_\beta B$ is compact as shown above, [F4] gives that it is trace class. Its basis trace in $(\psi_k)$ is absolutely convergent and equals the trace by [F7]. The $k$th diagonal entry is
$$\langle \rho_\beta B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle =e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle,$$
so this basis sum is the asserted numerator. Each term is bounded in modulus by $e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\|B\|$ by [F8] and [F9], giving the stated absolute bound. Division by $Z_\beta>0$ proves the expectation formula. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎
